title: How to Clean Silver Jewelry at Home
hook: Silver rings, chains and earrings turn dull and dark with time. You don't need a jeweler. Seven steps, three simple ways to remove tarnish at home, with soap, baking soda and aluminum foil. Twenty minutes, almost no cost. Stay for step four: the tarnish lifts off without any rubbing.
intro: Silver tarnishes when it reacts with sulfur in the air, in food, even on your skin. It's only a thin surface layer, and it comes off. A gentle wash is safe for almost everything; stronger methods are only for solid silver without delicate stones. Never clean a valuable heirloom without asking a jeweler first.
youNeed: Mild dish soap and warm water
youNeedNarration: You'll need mild dish soap and warm water, baking soda, aluminum foil, a soft toothbrush, and a silver polishing cloth. Use a glass or ceramic bowl for the hot water.
heroImagePrompt: Sterling silver rings and a necklace laid on a soft white cloth with a polishing cloth and a small bowl, bright window light, shallow depth of field, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Check what you're cleaning
steps.narration: Step one. Look closely at each piece. Is it solid sterling silver, often stamped 925, or silver-plated? Plating is a thin layer that can wear away with harsh rubbing. Check for gemstones, pearls, opals, turquoise or glued parts, because soft or porous stones are damaged by soaking and strong methods. Antique pieces with dark detail, called oxidized silver, are meant to look dark in the crevices, so don't remove it. If you're unsure, stick to method one. If a piece has a clasp or hinge that moves, test that it works before cleaning, and check again afterwards.
steps.imagePrompt: Several sterling silver rings and a bracelet on a white cloth, one with a 925 stamp visible, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Method one: soap and water
steps.narration: Step two. This safe, gentle method works for light tarnish and everyday dirt. Fill a bowl with warm, not boiling, water, and add a few drops of mild dish soap. Soak your jewelry for five minutes, then gently scrub with a soft toothbrush, paying attention to the chain links and the settings. Rinse under lukewarm water and pat dry. Close the sink drain first, so a small ring can't disappear. Always dry your hands and the piece well afterwards, so that no soap film stays behind to dull the shine. If some tarnish is still there, the next method goes one step further.
steps.imagePrompt: Silver rings in a bowl of soapy water with a soft toothbrush beside it, bright bathroom light, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Method two: baking soda paste
steps.narration: Step three. For moderate tarnish, mix three parts baking soda with one part water to make a thick paste. Apply it with a soft cloth or your fingertip, and rub gently along the piece, following the direction of any grain. Baking soda is a mild abrasive, so it removes tarnish without scratching sterling silver much. Use a soft toothbrush for detail. Rinse well, and dry with a soft cloth. Don't use this method on plated silver or soft stones. Do a small test spot first, just in case, and keep the pressure light, since silver is a soft metal.
steps.mistake: Using toothpaste as a silver polish
steps.imagePrompt: A silver ring being rubbed with white baking soda paste on a soft cloth, close-up, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Method three: foil and baking soda bath
steps.narration: Step four. For heavy tarnish on solid silver, line a glass or ceramic bowl with aluminum foil, shiny side up. Place the silver on the foil, so it touches. Add one tablespoon of baking soda per cup of very hot water, and pour it over the jewelry until covered. It will fizz. Wait two to five minutes, and the tarnish transfers to the foil. This method uses a chemical reaction, and it has a slight sulfur smell. Take care with hot water, and never leave it unattended with children or pets nearby. Let the water cool before pouring it away. Now for the part most people rush: rinsing and drying.
steps.mistake: Using the foil bath on pearls or antiques
steps.imagePrompt: Silver jewelry resting on aluminum foil in a glass bowl with hot water and baking soda, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Rinse and dry thoroughly
steps.narration: Step five. Remove the pieces from the water with tongs or a spoon, since they will be hot. Rinse each piece under cool running water to remove all residue. Dry with a soft cotton or microfiber cloth immediately. Moisture left in the links or the settings can bring the tarnish back sooner. For chains, use a cloth to wipe gently along the length. If a spot remains dark, repeat the method, rather than scrubbing harder. Pat, don't rub, near any delicate details. A hair dryer on a cool setting can help dry tricky links.
steps.imagePrompt: A soft white cloth drying a silver chain necklace on a table, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Polish to a shine
steps.narration: Step six. Use a silver polishing cloth, which is treated with a mild polish and tarnish inhibitor, to buff the piece. Rub gently, using long strokes, and turn the cloth to a clean section when it becomes dark. Do not use paper towels or tissues, which can leave scratches. Polish chains by pulling them through the folded cloth. A few minutes of buffing brings out the brightness, and leaves a protective layer. Keep your cloth in a zip bag between uses, so it doesn't pick up dust or moisture. One thing is left: stopping the tarnish from coming straight back.
steps.tip: Fold the cloth, pull chains through
steps.mistake: Polishing with tissue or paper towel
steps.imagePrompt: A silver polishing cloth buffing a shiny silver bracelet, close-up, soft light, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Store it to slow tarnish
steps.narration: Step seven. Tarnish returns fastest when silver meets air and moisture. Store each piece separately in a soft pouch, or a small zip bag with the air pressed out. Anti-tarnish bags or strips help. Keep silver away from bathrooms, and put it on last, after perfume, hairspray and lotion. Take it off before swimming, as chlorine damages silver, and before cleaning or cooking. Wearing silver often actually helps, because your skin oils keep it polished. A small piece of chalk in the pouch also absorbs moisture, which helps your silver stay bright longer.
steps.mistake: Storing silver in a humid bathroom
steps.imagePrompt: A jewelry box with small soft pouches holding silver rings and chains, tidy, soft daylight, photorealistic, no text

bonus.label: NOT WORKING?
bonus.title: If the tarnish stays
bonus.narration: If the tarnish stays, check your setup before you try again. The foil must touch the silver, the water must be very hot, and the piece must be fully covered. Repeat the bath once, and use a soft toothbrush on the crevices. Do not scrub harder, because silver is soft and scratches easily. If the piece is plated, stop, because thin plating can wear through.
bonus.imagePrompt: A darkened tarnished silver chain bracelet on a white cloth next to a ceramic bowl lined with aluminum foil, close-up. Photorealistic photograph for a home how-to video. Bright, tidy home interior, soft daylight. Adult hands, no face visible. 16:9 landscape format. No text, no letters, no logos, no watermark.

bonus.label: CALL A PRO
bonus.title: When to see a jeweler
bonus.narration: Some pieces are worth a visit to a jeweler. Antiques and family heirlooms deserve a professional's judgment before anything goes in water. Pearls, opals, turquoise and other soft stones need special care. A jeweler can also tighten loose stones, fix a weak clasp, and check the small metal prongs that hold a stone in place. Deep pitting or flaking plating needs a jeweler's opinion.
bonus.tip: Antiques and soft stones need a pro
bonus.imagePrompt: A jeweler's hands holding a silver ring with a small stone under a bright bench lamp, fine tools on a workbench. Photorealistic photograph for a home how-to video. Bright, tidy home interior, soft daylight. Adult hands, no face visible. 16:9 landscape format. No text, no letters, no logos, no watermark.

bonus.label: KEEP IT SHINING
bonus.title: Daily habits that slow tarnish
bonus.narration: Tarnish comes from sulfur in the air, and your daily habits matter. Put on perfume, hairspray and lotion before your jewelry, never after. Take silver off before swimming, because chlorine can damage it, and before showering or cleaning. Wiping each piece with a soft cloth after wearing removes oils and sweat. Keep silver away from rubber bands, wool and eggs, which all contain sulfur.
bonus.tip: Jewelry goes on last, off first
bonus.imagePrompt: A shiny silver necklace and earrings resting on a soft cloth on a dressing table, a perfume bottle placed to one side. Photorealistic photograph for a home how-to video. Bright, tidy home interior, soft daylight. Adult hands, no face visible. 16:9 landscape format. No text, no letters, no logos, no watermark.

mistakesToAvoid.narration: Here are the mistakes to avoid. First, using abrasive cleaners or toothpaste, which scratch silver, and leave dull marks. Second, soaking pieces with pearls, opals, turquoise or glued stones. They can crack or lose color. And third, cleaning oxidized or antique silver the same way, which removes the dark detail that gives it character. When in doubt, use soap and water, or ask a jeweler. If you own valuable or antique silver, a jeweler is always the safest choice.

recap.narration: Let's recap. Check what you're cleaning. Start with soap and water. Move up to a baking soda paste. Use the foil and baking soda bath on solid silver only. Rinse and dry thoroughly. Polish with a silver cloth. And store your silver to slow down tarnish. Seven steps, about twenty minutes, and your silver will shine again. Bonus sections cover what to do if the tarnish stays, when to see a jeweler, and the daily habits that keep silver shining.
items: Method three: foil and baking soda bath

outro: That's how you clean silver jewelry at home with three easy methods. If your silver is shining again, subscribe to WikiTube, because we publish a new how-to every single day. Tell us in the comments which piece you cleaned, and what you would like us to explain next. See you tomorrow. Share this with someone who has a drawer of dull silver.

metadata.title: How to Clean Silver Jewelry at Home (Don't Use Toothpaste)
metadata.description:
Dull, tarnished silver? In this step-by-step video you'll learn how to clean silver jewelry at home with three methods: gentle soap and water, a baking soda paste, and the aluminum foil and baking soda bath for heavy tarnish. We also explain which pieces to avoid, how to rinse, dry and polish silver, and how to store it so it stays bright for longer. Safe, simple and cheap. No special tools needed.

You'll need: mild dish soap and warm water, baking soda, aluminum foil, a soft toothbrush, a silver polishing cloth.

steps.title: Foil bath

steps.title: Rinse and polish
